about: Legacæstir (Chester): the Roman shell on the Dee in 793, the waste city of 893, the Lady's burh of 907, the mint and the Dublin harbour after it, to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/legacaestir.md and the spine. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not verified. Woven with the region on 7 Oct 2026: a later ale-wife, reeve and moneyer made real, ties run both ways, beats pointed at their cards (Data/encounters/northumbria_irish_sea_793.json).

ports.summary: A dead Roman fortress of red stone on a ridge in a bend of the Dee, far bigger than the handful of people who live under its south wall. In 793 it is King Offa's far shore: a church on the cliff, a landing, a few households, and lead that comes down from the hills to lie on the bank for want of a lawful buyer. A merchant comes for the lead, for salt from the wiches, and because nobody else comes; a hundred years on his heirs come for the mint and the Dublin men.
ports.seasons: The tide runs up past the town twice a day and a boat comes and goes on it or not at all; the sands in the river mouth shift after every winter gale. Lead and salt come down the tracks when the ground is dry, from Easter to Michaelmas. Saint John's feast at midsummer fills the church on the cliff, and after 907 Saint Werburgh's day in the dead of winter fills the minster. No fair is recorded here before 1066 (?).

history.text: About this year Æthelfrith of the Northumbrians beat the Welsh at the City of the Legions. Bede says he first cut down the monks of Bangor who had come to pray against him, about twelve hundred of them, and that only fifty got away.
history.source: Bede, Ecclesiastical History II.2 (paraphrased from memory (?)); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chester

history.text: They say King Æthelred of the Mercians founded the church of Saint John outside the walls in this year. It is a late tradition and no charter shows it.
history.source: Late tradition only: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John_the_Baptist's_Church,_Chester; VCH Cheshire 5.1 has 'possibly'

history.text: Offa is king of the Mercians. Nothing is recorded of the city in this year: no reeve, no market, no mint.
history.source: VCH Cheshire 5.1, 'Early medieval Chester 400-1230'; the silence is the fact

history.text: King Offa died on the 29th of July. His son Ecgfrith reigned a hundred and forty-one days after him, and then Coenwulf took the kingdom.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 794 for 796 (Ingram 1823); the day from the dossier (memory (?))

history.text: A Danish army rode day and night to a waste city in Wirral which is called Legaceaster. The English could not overtake them before they were inside; they lay about the place two days, took the cattle, burned the corn or let their horses eat it, and the Danes went on into Wales.
history.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 894 for 893 (Ingram 1823, who prints 'western' for 'waste'), paraphrased; VCH Cheshire 5.1

history.text: The Northmen were driven out of the fort at Dublin. Hingamund, one of their leaders, was beaten off Anglesey and came to the Lady of the Mercians, who gave him land in Wirral.
history.source: Fragmentary Annals of Ireland (not quoted), via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingimundr_(tenth_century); VCH Cheshire 5.1
Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 907 (Ingram 1823), as the dossier gives it

history.text: In 907 or about this year Hingamund and his men came against the town and were beaten off. An Irish saga-history tells it with boiling ale and beehives thrown from the wall; historians call the tale over-dramatised.
history.source: Fragmentary Annals of Ireland (not quoted), via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingimundr_(tenth_century); the date is not sure (?)

history.text: Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, died at Tamworth on the 12th of June, and her brother King Edward took Mercia.
The men of Chester rose with the Welsh. King Edward put them down, and died at Farndon up the Dee on the 17th of July.
history.source: VCH Cheshire 5.1 (from William of Malmesbury); the day from the dossier (memory (?))

history.text: King Edgar gave land to the minster of Saint Werburgh: the first sure word that the minster stands.
About this year somebody buried a pot of some five hundred pennies with ingots and cut jewellery by the south-west corner of the walls, and never came back for it.
history.source: The Castle Esplanade hoard, found 1950: VCH Cheshire 5.1; the count from the dossier (memory (?))

history.text: King Edgar 'led all his marine force to Chester; and there came to meet him six kings; and they all covenanted with him, that they would be his allies by sea and by land.'
'The county of Chester was plundered by the pirate-army of the North.'
King Æthelred wasted Cumberland. His ships were to come round from Chester to meet him and could not, and harried the Isle of Man instead.
Edmund the ætheling and Earl Uhtred of the Northumbrians plundered Staffordshire, Shrewsbury and Chester.
Earl Leofric died. He and his wife Godgifu had enriched both the minsters of the town.
Earl Harold rode from Chester against Gruffudd of the Welsh at Rhuddlan and burned his hall and his ships.
The city has 487 houses, seven moneyers, twelve judges, and pays the king forty-five pounds and three timbers of marten skins a year.
history.source: Domesday Book, Cheshire, the state before 1066, via VCH Cheshire 5.1

eras.text: Offa's far shore. Red walls with nobody on them, a priest and his church on the cliff, a few households under the south gate and an ale-house in the corner of the old baths. Lead lies stacked on the bank because the Frankish ports are shut to English goods. Welsh herdsmen come over the ford with honey and go back with salt, and nobody takes a toll because nobody has been told to.

The kings of the Mercians change and grow smaller, and the city does not change at all. A wall stone falls now and then. The priest's successors bury the same few families. From the 860s the talk at the landing is of a heathen army that does not go home, and in 874 it drives the Mercian king over the sea; the lead goes on coming down, a little less each year.

A waste city. In 893 a Danish army lies inside the walls and the English burn the corn round it. After 902 Northmen out of Dublin sit on the Wirral shore by the Lady's leave, with Irish among them, and their boats come up on the tide to sell and to look. Nobody is sure who the walls belong to.

The Lady's burh. The walls are mended, a new length runs down to the river, and there is a gravel road inside the west wall. A minster rises in the north-east corner with a saint brought from the south, there is a market at the old cross-roads and a mint whose pennies carry no king's head. The reeve asks every hull whose leave she came by. In 924 the town rises with the Welsh, and a king dies of putting it down.

The mint's great years. More moneyers strike here than in London for a while, and their pennies lie thick in Dublin and Man. Dublin skippers bring marten skins and take salt, pots and people. A church of Saint Bridget stands by the river for the Irish and the Northmen, and huts with bowed walls line the street down to the landing. About 965 a man buries his silver by the wall and does not come back.

King Edgar comes with his fleet and six kings swear to him; within a lifetime the tale has eight of them rowing his boat. His new coin leaves the town five moneyers where there were twenty. In 980 ships out of the north plunder the shire, and in 1000 the king's fleet goes out from here and comes back with nothing but Manx cattle.

The earls' town. Leofric and Godgifu give to both minsters; a church of Saint Olaf goes up for the Northmen after 1030; four in ten of the moneyers have Norse or Irish names. Earl Ælfgar pays off his hired Irish fleet at the landing, Harold rides out from here against the Welsh king, and in the last winter of the story Harold's queen is brought here for safety.

sites.name: The landing under the south wall
sites.see: A shelf of red mud and shingle on the north bank of the Dee, with a few tarred boats drawn up and a hide boat upside down on stakes like a black bowl. Behind it the ground climbs to a wall of red squared stone with a gap where a gate was, and the light comes down the river from the west. It smells of tide mud and wet rope, and the only sounds are curlews and the water turning.
sites.source: The 'early harbour' on the river bank south of the fortress, below the later Lower Bridge Street, where the clearest pre-Conquest finds come from: VCH Cheshire 5.1. The weir is Norman, so the tide ran past the town (inference)

sites.name: The bank where things are bartered
sites.see: A trodden patch above the tide line where a plank lies across two Roman column drums. On it, on a good day: a crock of honey, a sack of salt, two cheeses, a bundle of hides. A Welshman and an Englishwoman bargain with their fingers because neither has the other's tongue. Smoke from three hearths drifts across it.
sites.source: Invented for play: whether any market was held here in 793 is not known (?). The only sign of goods from oversea is a few Carolingian jar sherds on the river bank: VCH Cheshire 5.1

sites.name: The lead stack
sites.see: A lean-to of turf and old roof tiles against the foot of the wall, and under it grey pigs of lead stacked like loaves, each as long as a forearm and as heavy as a calf. A two-wheeled cart with a broken felloe stands beside it. Everything near is dusted grey, the grass grows thin, and the man who sits there has grey in the creases of his hands.
sites.source: The spine's hook (thread black_stones): lead from the hills behind comes down to the Dee. Roman lead was mined in the hills west of the estuary and pigs of it have been found at Chester (memory (?)); working there in 793 is not attested (?). Lead for church roofs and salt pans: Design/content/economy/stone_metal_arms.md

sites.name: The red walls and the south gate
sites.see: A wall of great red blocks without mortar, three men high where it stands whole, with ash trees rooted in the top and one arch of a gateway still up. Through the arch a straight street runs north between humps of bramble that were barracks. After 907 the gaps are filled with new work, a timber gate hangs in the arch, and men walk the top.
sites.source: The Roman walls about 4.9 m high, standing but unrepaired until 907; then mended and a wall probably run from the south-east corner to the river: VCH Cheshire 5.1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_city_walls

sites.name: Saint John's on the red cliff
sites.see: A small stone church on the cliff above the river, east of the walls, built of blocks carried from the ruin next to it: a great oval hollow in the ground, grassed over, with one curve of stone seats showing like ribs. Jackdaws live in the hollow. From the church door the river shines below, and inside it smells of tallow and damp stone. After 907 a masons' yard beside it cuts round-headed crosses out of the red rock.
sites.source: St John's outside the walls beside the amphitheatre, tied to the bishops of Lichfield; the masons' yard and the circle-headed crosses of 'Redcliff' stone (10th to 11th century (?)); the amphitheatre 95.7 by 87.2 m, robbed for stone: VCH Cheshire 5.1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_Roman_Amphitheatre. The size of the church in 793 is not known (?)

sites.name: The ale-house in the old baths
sites.see: Inside the south gate a Roman wall stands higher than any tree, with a round arch in it and a roof of thatch slung across one corner. Under the thatch are a hearth, three benches, casks on a stone floor patterned in small coloured squares, and a woman who looks at every face twice. It is warm, it smells of malt and woodsmoke, and swallows go in and out over the drinkers' heads.
sites.source: The legionary bath-house, whose walls once rose 16 m: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deva_Victrix. How much stood in 793 is not known, and the ale-house is invented (?). Ale-wives and the bad-ale fine are in the customs of the city before 1066: Domesday Book via VCH Cheshire 5.1

sites.name: The crossing to the south bank
sites.see: A flat boat on a rope of twisted hide, and at low water a line of stones a careful man can walk. On the far bank a cliff of red rock has been cut back in steps by old quarrymen, and on one face, small and worn, is a carved woman with a spear and a bird at her shoulder. Cattle stand in the shallows. The track beyond goes to Wales.
sites.source: The Roman quarry across the river at Handbridge with its rock-cut shrine of Minerva, still there today: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deva_Victrix. A bridge stood before 1066 (Domesday); none is attested for 793, so the game has a ferry and a low-water ford (?)

sites.name: Henwald's Lowe
sites.see: A round green mound in the rough pasture north-east of the walls, twice a man's height, with a thorn tree on it bent away from the sea wind. Sheep lie on its lee side. From the top the whole red square of the fortress shows, and the river, and the hills of the Welsh blue behind.
sites.source: Henwald's Lowe, 'Henwald's barrow', a mound north-east of the walls, perhaps an early lord's grave: VCH Cheshire 5.1. Who Henwald was is not known

sites.name: Saint Bridget's by the river
sites.see: A timber church with a shingle roof, south of the walls on the street that goes down to the landing, and round it long huts whose side walls bow outward like a boat's. Men with Norse names and Irish mothers stand at the door after Mass and talk of Dublin prices. A rush cross hangs over the lintel, and the street smells of peat smoke and stockfish.
sites.source: St Bridget's, the Irish and Norse settlers' church south of the fortress, probably from their arrival; bow-sided huts of Scandinavian kind on Lower Bridge Street: VCH Cheshire 5.1. Its first year is not known (?)

sites.name: The Lady's hall
sites.see: A long timber hall with a new thatch, set among the bramble humps inside the walls, with a yard of raked gravel and a line of spears in a rack by the door. Carts of stone and lime go past it all day to the wall. Inside, a high seat with an empty chair beside it, a board with tally sticks, and a woman's voice asking short questions.
sites.source: Timber halls and sunken huts of the 10th century inside the fortress at Hamilton Place, Crook Street and Hunter Street: VCH Cheshire 5.1. That one of them was the Lady's is the game's (?). After 918 it is the reeve's, then the ealdorman's and the earl's

sites.name: The reeve's board at the water gate
sites.see: A trestle under a penthouse roof where the new wall comes down to the river, with a balance, a measure for ale and a peg rail hung with lead tags on cords. Two reeves' men sit there, the king's and the earl's, and do not much like each other. Every bale that comes up from the landing passes the board, and so does every skin.
sites.source: The customs of the city before 1066: leave to come and go, 4 pence a load on leaving (two parts the king's, one the earl's), marten skins shown to the reeve first: Domesday Book, quoted from memory by the dossier (?), outline in VCH Cheshire 5.1. They describe 1066; the game lets them begin with the burh in 907 (?). A lead customs tag from Chester dies of Eadwig's reign was found at Coppergate, York: VCH

sites.name: The market at the cross
sites.see: Where the two straight streets of the old fortress meet there is a small church of Saint Peter, and before its door the market: grey-black pots stacked in straw, salt in sacks, cloth, combs of antler, disc brooches on a board, and on some days a rope of people for sale. Dublin men in fur-edged cloaks walk through it, pricing everything.
sites.source: St Peter's at the cross of the Roman streets, by tradition dedicated in 907; Chester-ware pots, salt, cloth, brooches and slaves out, marten skins in; bone and antler working at Abbey Green: VCH Cheshire 5.1

sites.name: The moneyers' benches
sites.see: A row of low lock-up sheds near the market, each with a block of oak set in the floor and an iron die standing in it. A man sets a blank on the die, a boy holds the upper iron, and the hammer comes down once. It rings like a small bell, twenty times in the space of a prayer. Charcoal smoke, hot metal, and a pot of clippings nobody takes his eyes off.
sites.source: A mint in north-west Mercia from about 890, most likely here; about 16 moneyers by 916-918 and at least 25 under Æthelstan; an ingot mould from Lower Bridge Street: VCH Cheshire 5.1. The mint's house has not been found, so its place is the game's (?)

sites.name: Saint Werburgh's minster
sites.see: In the north-east corner of the walls, a stone church with a timber porch and a row of canons' houses, all new and all built of old red blocks. Inside, a shrine with a cloth over it and a lamp that is never let go out. On the saint's day in the dead of winter geese are driven up the street to be blessed, complaining the whole way.
sites.source: The minster certainly there by 958, probably founded or refounded by Æthelflæd after 907 with Werburgh's body brought from Hanbury (the date 875 is late and unreliable); a warden and twelve canons in 1066: VCH Cheshire 5.1. Werburgh's feast 3 February and her goose: Goscelin, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werburgh. The blessing of geese is invented (?)

people.name: Eadhelm
people.trait: The priest of Saint John's: schooled at the bishop's house, sent here young, and never called back. Kind, exact about feasts, starved of anything to read.
people.want: A leaf of Bede with the story of his own city on it; a sound roof; somebody to talk Latin with before he forgets it.
people.fear: That he will die here and the next priest will not be able to read the two books he has.
people.voice: Gentle and dry. Starts sentences with what the day's saint did, then comes to the point.
people.looks: Near fifty, thin, tonsured grey hair, a patched brown tunic to the ankle and a wooden cross on a thong; ink on no finger, which he minds.
knows: every household under the wall, and who is owed what
what Bede is said to have written of the City of the Legions and the monks of Bangor, at second hand
the feasts and fasts, and which days a bale should not be opened
the road to the bishop at Lichfield and who goes on it
news of the church: he will be the one who tells the town of Lindisfarne, once he is told

ties.note: one letter a year goes to York by any hand that offers; he asks each time for a leaf and each time gets a blessing
never met him; has a letter of his copied at third hand and reads it to the households on feast days
a scribe he has never seen, who once sent him a quill and a recipe for ink
the lead man has promised him a roof when a buyer pays; the priest has promised him prayers on account
she feeds him in Lent on what the rule allows and a little that it does not

lines.greet: God keep you. A sail on this river is a thing to write down, if I had anything to write on. Come in out of the wind.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian again. I said a Mass for your keel at Candlemas. It seems to have held.
rumour: They say King Æthelred of the Mercians built this church a hundred years back. I say it too. Nobody has ever shown me the writing.
The Welsh who cross the ford bless themselves at the north wall. Twelve hundred monks died out there, praying. They have not forgotten, and do not care which English king it was.
My bishop sits at Lichfield, four days off. He was made an archbishop for King Offa's sake. It has not made the road any shorter.
lines.news: Saint Cuthbert's church robbed, and the brothers killed? Say it again, slowly. I must tell it to forty people and I will not get it wrong.
lines.saying: The City of the Legions, and I have nine households and a goat. God enjoys a joke about pride.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and mind the sands at the river mouth. If you pass a house with books, remember there is one here without.

people.source: Invented. Clergy at St John's in 793 are 'a fair guess and only a guess' (dossier (?)). Lichfield an archbishopric 787 to 803 under Hygeberht: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 785 (memory (?)). The Bangor monks: Bede II.2

people.name: Beornoth
people.trait: The lead man: digs it, melts it and carts it down from the hills with two sons and an ox. Patient as his metal, and as hard to move on a price.
people.want: A buyer oversea who pays in silver, not in the king's thanks; and to be rid of the stack before it sinks into the bank.
people.fear: The king's reeve remembering that the hills are the king's; a wet summer; his chest, which has begun to ache.
people.voice: Slow. Counts on his fingers while he talks and never loses the count.
people.looks: Forty, broad and stooped, grey dust in his beard and the creases of his hands, a leather apron scorched at the hem, a short iron bar for levering pigs.
knows: the price of lead here and what it fetches at the wiches for salt pans
that a Frankish abbot who keeps tolls has asked King Offa's people for roof lead, and that it cannot lawfully cross while the ports are shut
how to stow lead in a small boat so she still sails
the tracks west into the hills, and the old workings where Roman pigs turn up
who in the south takes the king's share

ties.note: the abbot's token came up the road two summers ago with a promise of silver; forty pigs have waited on the bank for it ever since
the king's reeve at Lundenwic takes the king's part of the lead, when a cart gets that far (?)
the same abbot, where he sits at his toll
a roof for Saint John's, promised at his wife's burial
his wife's brother; they have not agreed about anything since the wedding and work together every week

lines.greet: You are looking at the pigs. Everyone does. Lift one before you ask the price. It saves talk.
lines.greet_again: The boat that carries more than she looks. I kept six pigs back for you, in case you came.
rumour: A Frankish abbot wants lead for his roofs. He is King Offa's friend. His own king has shut the ports, so his roofs leak. That is kings for you.
The old people cut their names into their lead. I dig up their pigs by the old workings. Better cast than mine. I melt them anyway.
Lead goes to the salt boilers for their pans, and to churches. Nobody else wants a thing so heavy. That is why I am poor.
lines.peace: The ports are open? Then the price is up a penny a pig since this morning. Do not look at me so. You brought the news yourself.
lines.saying: Lead is honest. It weighs what it weighs, and nobody steals it twice.
lines.farewell: Stow them low, along the keel. If she sinks, at least you will know why.

people.source: Invented, to carry the spine's hook (thread black_stones). Charlemagne's wish for English lead and the closed ports: goods_793.json (lead) and the spine. Lead mining west of the Dee in 793 is not attested (?)

people.name: Wigburh
people.trait: Keeps the ale-house in the corner of the old baths. Forgets no face, no debt and no kindness, and says which is which.
people.want: Custom from the river; her son home from the king's host on the Welsh border; malt that is not half chaff.
people.fear: The great wall coming down on her casks in a gale; a brewing gone sour with strangers in the house.
people.voice: Quick and dry. Asks two questions before she pours and remembers both answers for years.
people.looks: Early thirties, strong forearms, a linen head-cloth and a madder-red gown kilted up, a bunch of keys and a wooden dipper at her belt.
knows: everyone who has come up the river in ten years, what they drank and what they owed
the week's barter at the bank: honey, salt, hides, cheese
which crewmen are for hire and which should not be
the talk from the Welsh side, through a herdsman who courts her niece
what Thiadbod of Dorestad asked about when he lay here

ties.note: her brother; he drinks free and pays in fish
she keeps his Lent honest and his belly from his backbone
he lay here one summer, paid in clipped pennies and asked too closely about the lead; she has kept one of the pennies to show
your lookout owes her for a cup from his first night here; she means to collect it for the rest of his life
an ale-wife of the king's wic; they send each other word and barm by the lead carts

lines.greet: Sit by the warm wall. Romans built it to heat water. I use it to keep ale from the frost. Who are you, and who answers for you?
lines.greet_again: Your bench is where you left it. That lookout of yours still owes me for a cup. I have not forgotten his face.
lines.remember: You came at lambing time two years back, with a wet cargo and a dry crew. I remember dry crews.
rumour: Two Welshmen came over the ford with honey and went back with salt. That is the market this week. Do not tell the king. He will want a toll.
A stone fell from the bath wall at Martinmas and killed a pig. The priest says it is a warning. The pig's owner says it is a debt.
King Offa is digging a ditch to keep the Welsh out. My sister's man digs on it. He says the Welsh come at night and help, the other way.
lines.saying: Bad ale is a sin you can taste. For the others you must take the priest's word.
lines.farewell: Come back before the casks are empty. I brew at each new moon, and I count who drinks.

people.source: Invented. Ale-wives and the fine for bad ale (the dung-stool or 4 shillings) are in the city's customs before 1066: Domesday via VCH Cheshire 5.1. Offa's dyke is attributed to him by Asser a century later; its date is not sure (?)

people.name: Osfrith
people.trait: Fisherman, ferryman and the only pilot on the Dee. Has been wrong about the sands twice in his life and names both days.
people.want: A second boat; a boy to teach the channel to, since his own went to the lead.
people.fear: Fog on a spring tide with a stranger's keel under him.
people.voice: Flat, a little scornful, as a man is who is always asked the same thing. Warms up when a boat is handled well.
people.looks: Late thirties, lean and weathered, bare legs muddy to the knee, a sealskin cap, a sounding pole taller than himself with notches cut in it.
knows: the channel down to the sea: tight to the Wirral shore, and where the sand has moved since the last gale
the island in the river mouth and when it can be walked to
the old beach market on the tip of Wirral where no king's man stands
which hide boats on the river are Welsh and which Irish, and what each carries
the hours of the tide by the moon, to the width of a hand

ties.note: his sister; the only person who can make him wait
his sister's husband's brother by the lead man's reckoning, a fool by his own; he ferries the pigs all the same
took two of the abbot's monks up the river in a hide boat once, bound for Lichfield with a book (?); they prayed the whole way and he approved of it
has never met the Frisian pilot, but skippers carry each one's sayings to the other and both think the other must be a sound man
the boatman of Columba's island, met at the saint's feast: brings sealskin, takes lead, and gives the rocks more room than seems manly

lines.greet: You came up on the flood with nobody aboard who knows this river. Either God loves you or the sands were asleep. Next time, ask for me.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. Still afloat. I will take you down on tomorrow's ebb. The channel has moved a boat's length since you saw it.
rumour: Keep to the Wirral shore going out, close enough to count the cows. The Welsh side is all sand, and the sand moves at night.
There is an island in the river mouth with a holy man's hut. At low water you can walk to it. At high water you had better like the holy man.
Past the point is a beach where boats have traded since before the Romans. No king's man stands there. I never told you so.
lines.saying: The tide is the only lord here who comes twice a day and takes nothing.
lines.farewell: Ebb at first light. Be on the bank or be here another day. The river does not wait, and I wait less.

people.source: Invented. The estuary, Hilbre Island and the channel along the Wirral side: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Dee,_Wales. Meols as a beach market since the Iron Age: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meols. A cell on Hilbre in 793 is not attested (?)

people.name: Hingamund
people.trait: A sea-lord with too many mouths behind him: driven from Dublin, beaten off Anglesey, living on a gift of sand. Tired, courteous, and watched by his own young men.
people.want: Good land, and the walled town that looks down on it.
people.fear: A hungry winter; the day his young men stop asking him and start telling him.
people.voice: Says less than he means, slowly, and smiles at the wrong places.
people.looks: About fifty, heavy-shouldered, a grey-fair beard in two plaits, a faded blue cloak with a silver ring pin of Irish work, a sword he does not take off to eat.
knows: how the fort at Dublin fell and who took it
the Wirral shore, its landings and how many boats lie on each
which of his people are Irish and Christian and might listen to the Lady
what hides, ale and honey fetch among people who came away with nothing
the sea road to Man and the Ribble

ties.note: she gave him the land he stands on; he asked for it saying he was tired of war
the king of Leinster who took the fort from him in 902
a man who crossed with his people and went inside the walls to earn; they still drink together (?)
a youth who followed him out of the fort as far as Man, and then went to the monks; he bears no grudge, having lost better men to worse

lines.greet: A merchant. Good. I have had enough of kings this year. Three have shown me the door, and one of them was a woman.
lines.greet_again: You again. Sit. You are the only man on this river who sells to me without counting my ships first.
rumour: The Irish kings took the fort at the black pool. We left ships half built on the strand. I think about those ships.
The Lady gave us land by the sea. Sand, mostly. She is generous with sand.
There is a town with walls and a lady whose lord is sick. My young men can count. I tell them to go and count the walls again.
lines.saying: A man who is tired of war should not live in sight of a rich town.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you see smoke over the red walls some morning, lie in the river mouth until it clears.

people.source: Hingamund (Ingimundr): Fragmentary Annals of Ireland (not quoted; paraphrased from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingimundr_(tenth_century)) and the Welsh annals for Anglesey. His age, looks and words are invented. The annal calls his men pagans; the Wirral settlers' church of St Bridget suggests many were not (?)

people.name: Æthelflæd
people.trait: The Lady of the Mercians, King Alfred's daughter: builds a fortress a year and knows the cost of each to the penny.
people.want: The wall whole from the corner to the river, and to know what lies in the river mouth before it moves.
people.fear: Dublin's Northmen and York's joining hands across her land.
people.voice: Asks short questions and listens to the whole answer. Thanks people by name.
people.looks: About forty, straight-backed, a plain dark wool gown with a gold-wire border, a white head-cloth, keys and a small knife at her girdle; lime dust on her shoes.
knows: every burh of Mercia, and which is next
the terms she gave the men from Ireland, and how far she trusts them
who may trade at the cross and what the reeve may ask
that the Irish among the Northmen are Christians, and what that is worth
the saint's journey from Hanbury

ties.note: she gave him land because a fed neighbour is cheaper than a siege, and mended the wall in case she was wrong
her moneyer; she likes that he has been where her enemies come from
the Northman who sat in her father's hall when she was a girl and told of the far north; she still has a walrus tooth from him (?)
another of her father's sea-farers; she asks merchants whether he lives

lines.greet: You came by water past Wirral. How many ships on the north shore, hauled up or afloat? Then we will talk about your cargo.
lines.greet_again: The merchant who counts. Good. Count for me again. What lies in the river mouth this month?
rumour: My lord is sick and the wall is broken. I can mend only one of them. So I mend the wall.
I gave the men from Ireland land because a fed neighbour is cheaper than a siege. I may be wrong. The wall is in case I am wrong.
The saint is come to us from Hanbury, out of the heathen's road. A town with a wall wants somebody inside worth guarding.
lines.saying: A burh is a wall, a market and a church. Leave one out and you have built a sheepfold.
lines.farewell: Go in the king's peace and mine. Bring me true word of the river mouth and you will not pay at my gate.

people.source: Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, born about 870, died 12 June 918 at Tamworth; refounded Chester 907: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Æthelflæd; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (Mercian Register). Her husband Æthelred died 911 and was ill in the siege story. Her words, looks and presence here on any given day are invented. The role 'count' stands for a ruling lady: see the report's needs

people.name: Irfara
people.trait: A moneyer whose name means the Ireland-farer, and who is pleased with it. Quick hands, quicker eye for bad silver.
people.want: Broken arm-rings and foreign coin to melt; his pennies taken without a second look from Dublin to York.
people.fear: A light penny with his name on it.
people.voice: Fast and cheerful. Puts a coin in your hand to make each point and takes it back after.
people.looks: Thirty-five, wiry, cropped fair hair, burn scars on both forearms, a leather apron, a folding balance on a cord round his neck.
knows: what Dublin silver is worth here, by weight and by the nick
why the town's pennies carry no king's head
which moneyers at the benches strike true
the crossing to Dublin and Man: he made it for years
that dies are cut here for other Mercian towns

ties.note: strikes for the Lady and after her for King Edward
came over the water in the same bad year (?)
the king back in Dublin from 917, whose men pay in hacked silver and call his pennies thin
never met him: but the trick of the three reckonings came north from a Dorestad moneyer's house, and he teaches it as his own
the Frank at York who strikes for the Danish kings; each bites the other's pennies first

lines.greet: They call me the Ireland-farer. I went, I came back, and now I sit and hit silver with a hammer. It is the better trade. What have you brought?
lines.greet_again: Your silver was good last time. I nicked every piece of it, you understand. But it was good.
rumour: No king's head on our pennies. A cross, a name, the town. The Dublin men like them plain. They only weigh them anyway.
We cut dies here for Derby and Tamworth. If a penny from there is ugly, that was my work on a Monday.
My name is on every penny I strike. If one is found light, nobody asks the penny.
lines.saying: Silver has no memory. That is why they put a man's name on it.
lines.farewell: Go well. Take my pennies west, they are known there. Bring back arm-rings, broken ones. I do not care whose arms.

people.source: Irfara, moneyer at Chester under Edward the Elder, a Norse nickname, 'the Ireland-farer': VCH Cheshire 5.1. Only the name on the coins is real; his years, his people and every word are invented (?). No king's head before 970 and dies cut for Derby and Tamworth: VCH (the reign for the dies is not given (?))

people.name: Beorhtwine
people.trait: The king's reeve at the water gate: fair, tired, and proof against every trick a Dublin skipper knows, since he has seen each twice.
people.want: The king's farm paid in full at Michaelmas, the skins counted, and one quiet year.
people.fear: Ships that come without leave, and answering for them.
people.voice: Recites the custom like a prayer he has stopped hearing, then says one sharp thing of his own.
people.looks: Middle-aged, stout, a clipped grey beard, a good green cloak with a round silver brooch, a bundle of lead tags on cords at his belt.
knows: the custom of the port: leave, the four pence, the marten skins, the days no bale is opened
every hull from Dublin and Man by her sail
what goes over the hills to York under his seal
the twelve judges and which of them can be bored into mercy
after 973: how many kings came, by his own count

ties.note: the king in Dublin whose skippers he fines each summer and dines each winter
his fellow at York, who reads the lead tags at the other end of the hill road (?)
his mother's father, he says, when a Northman doubts his right to count their skins (?)
the earl at York, to whom he sends word of Dublin fleets by the hill road, and from whom he hears of the Humber
fined her four shillings for a thin brewing, and still drinks at her wall; neither mentions it

lines.greet: Whose leave did you come in by? Say the king's and I will believe you once. Four pence a load when you go, and we are friends.
lines.greet_again: I know the boat. Lie where you lay before. If there are marten skins aboard, I see them before anyone. As before.
rumour: The Dublin men bring marten skins and take salt, pots and people. I look at the skins first. What the king does not want, the earl may want.
A woman sold bad ale on Saturday. Four shillings or the dung-stool. She chose the stool. She says the shillings would last longer.
The king was here with every ship he owns. Six kings came and swore to him. I counted six. Ask me again in ten years and hear how many.
lines.raid: Ships out of the north went through the shire like fire through thatch. A man by the wall hid his pennies under the floor. He has not come to dig.
lines.saying: Open no bale between Saturday's noon and Monday's light. God rests then. The bishop's man does not.
lines.farewell: Four pence a load, two parts the king's and one the earl's. Go in peace, and come back the same way.

people.source: Invented; no reeve of Chester is named for these years. The customs are those of the city before 1066 in Domesday Book, quoted from memory by the dossier and needing a check (?): VCH Cheshire 5.1 for the outline. Six kings: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 973. The raid: Chronicle 980. The hoard: Pemberton's Parlour, VCH

people.name: Wigflaed
people.trait: Keeps the ale-house in the old baths as her mothers did: brews for Dublin skippers and king's reeves alike, and trades in salt on the side through a woman by the Liffey.
people.want: Good malt, quiet Saturdays, and salt from the wiches at the price her mother paid.
people.fear: The four shillings or the dung-stool for a bad brewing; ships out of the north on a spring tide.
people.voice: Brisk and dry; counts in pennies and in cups; has a Norse word for every kind of drunk.
people.looks: Forty, strong forearms, a linen head-cloth and a green gown kilted up, a round silver brooch that was a Dublin skipper's pledge and never redeemed, keys and a wooden dipper at her belt.
knows: which Dublin and Manx skippers are in the river, what they owe and what they carry
the custom of the port: the four pence, the marten skins, the closed Saturday
the price of Droitwich salt this month, and who is sending it west
the tale of the six kings, and how many they have become at her own benches

ties.note: the ale-wife by the Liffey ford: they send each other salt, barm and word of whose ship is coming
the reeve fined her four shillings for a thin brewing and still drinks here; neither mentions it
five or six lives back: the house, the keys and the warm wall came down the women

lines.greet: Sit by the warm wall. It has kept ale from the frost since before anybody here had a king. What are you drinking, and whose leave did you come in by?
lines.greet_again: You again. Your bench is free and your last cup is paid, which is more than I can say for half Dublin.
rumour: Six kings came and swore to King Edgar on this river. By Martinmas it was seven at my benches. I expect eight by Easter.
A woman up the street sold bad ale and chose the dung-stool over the four shillings. She says the shillings would have lasted longer.
There is an ale-wife by the ford at Dublin who sends me word of every ship that sails for the Dee. I know your cargo before the reeve does. Do not tell him.
lines.saying: A reeve counts what comes up the river. I count what goes down a throat. Mine is the surer tally.
lines.farewell: Go down on the ebb, and not on a Saturday after noon. The bishop's man is thirstier than the king's, and twice as sharp.

people.source: invented: made real in the weave of 7 Oct 2026 to answer duiblinn.json's tie from the ale-wife Affraic ('a woman who brews by the Dee'). Ale-wives and the fine for bad ale, four shillings or the dung-stool, are in the customs of the city before 1066 (Domesday, by VCH Cheshire 5.1 (?)). The six kings: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 973. Name: Wig- + -flaed, after the Wigburh of 793.

people.name: Wynstan
people.trait: The king's reeve at the water gate under three kings and one earl's house: courteous, immovable, and sure that every Dublin ship carries something she has not shown him.
people.want: The king's farm paid in full, the marten skins seen first, and Dublin's new pennies kept out of his chest until somebody tells him what they weigh.
people.fear: A fleet in the Dee with the earl away; and being the reeve who let the dies out of the town.
people.voice: Formal and unhurried, exact about pennies; says the custom word for word, and then asks one question that is not in it.
people.looks: Fifty, lean, a clipped iron-grey beard, a dark blue cloak with a disc brooch, lead tags on a cord and a small folding balance at his belt, a hound that goes everywhere with him.
knows: the custom of the port, to the quarter of a penny, and every way it has been dodged
what a Dublin penny weighs this year against the king's
which moneyers at the benches have Norse names and Irish cousins
who is building ships at Dublin, and for whose war

ties.note: the king at Dublin thinks four pence a load and first sight of the skins too much; the reeve thinks the king's pennies too new; each is partly right
buys the Dublin wright's ships for the earl and fines the skippers who bring them up the river without leave; the wright has stopped expecting sense
watches the moneyer who is said to have sold a worn die's pattern over the water, and cannot prove it
the island skipper pays his four pence without argument and brings news of the earl in Orkney

lines.greet: By whose leave do you come up the Dee? Say it plainly. Four pence a load when you go. If there are marten skins aboard, I see them before any man.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian house. Your tags were in order the last time. I looked. I shall look again. Do not take it to heart.
rumour: The king at Dublin has struck pennies with his own name, copied from ours. I weighed one. It was honest. That is what worries me.
A Dublin skipper came up the river without leave and paid his forty shillings like a man buying a horse. He will do it again. They reckon it into the price.
The earl buys his ships from the Dublin yard, and I fine the skippers who deliver them. It is the custom. Nobody has yet explained it to the earl.
lines.saying: Leave is asked before and paid for after. A man who mixes the two pays twice.
lines.farewell: Four pence a load, two parts the king's and one the earl's. Go down on the ebb, and not between Saturday's noon and Monday.

people.source: invented: made real in the weave of 7 Oct 2026 to answer duiblinn.json's ties from King Sitriuc and the wright Asgrimr ('the king's reeve at the Dee') and its story duiblinn.christmas_ounce. The customs are the city's before 1066 in Domesday (VCH Cheshire 5.1 (?)); the first Dublin pennies, copied from King Æthelred's, are of about 997 (chronicle_793.json 997-dublin-coins). Name: Wyn- + -stan.

people.name: Hallmund
people.trait: A moneyer of the Chester benches with a Norse name and an Irish wife's cousins in Dublin: strikes the king's pennies true, and sees no harm in telling a neighbour king how it is done.
people.want: Silver to strike, a quiet reeve, and to be paid by two kings for one craft.
people.fear: The reeve's eye on his die box; a hand lost for a thing he calls a kindness.
people.voice: Easy and low; talks of dies as a groom talks of horses; changes the subject when the water gate is named.
people.looks: Forty, short, quick hands, a singed yellow beard, a leather apron, a hammer in his belt and a bunch of small iron punches on a ring.
knows: how a die is cut, hardened and worn out, and what a worn one is worth to a man who has none
what the king's penny weighs this issue, and when it will next be called in
which Dublin men ask about dies, and which only about pennies
what gold fetches at the goldsmiths' end of the street, by the ounce

ties.note: sold the king at Dublin a bag of new pennies and the pattern of a worn die, and calls it trade
the reeve watches his die box; he watches the reeve's dog
claims the Ireland-farer for a grandfather, as half the benches do (?)

lines.greet: Silver to change? Put it down. English, Dublin, Frankish: it all goes into the same pot. Only the king's comes out.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the honest purse. Sit. I shall take the king's share and nothing for myself. Today.
rumour: The king at Dublin wants pennies with his own head on them. He has the silver. He has not the dies. A die is only iron, with a little knowledge in it.
They call the pennies in every few years and strike them new, a little lighter. The king gains a penny in six. I gain a sore arm.
Gold is wanted over the water at Christmas, an ounce to a house. A man who had gold at Martinmas could name his price in silver by Advent.
lines.saying: A die wears out. What it knows does not. That is the part they forget to lock up.
lines.farewell: Go well. If you see the reeve's dog on the bank, the reeve is behind it. He always is.

people.source: invented: made real in the weave of 7 Oct 2026 to answer the link 'legacaestir.moneyer' of duiblinn.json's story duiblinn.christmas_ounce ('at the Dee the moneyers have Norse and Irish names; one will sell a worn die's pattern, if the reeve is not told'). Chester was among the busiest mints of the tenth century, and the first Dublin pennies of about 997 copy King Æthelred's (chronicle_793.json 997-dublin-coins); that a Chester moneyer helped is a guess (?). The name, from attested Norse parts (Hall-, -mund), is not meant for any moneyer named on the coins (?).

stories.title: Lead for the abbot's roof
stories.summary: Forty pigs of lead lie on the bank of the Dee, promised to a Frankish abbot whose king has shut his ports to English goods. A Frisian hull is not an English one, and a toll man's word is all that stands between the stack and the roof.
stories.picture: A grey stack of lead pigs under a turf lean-to against a red Roman wall, a stooped man with an iron bar beside it, a small boat on the mud below, evening.

beats.text: Beornoth shows the stack and the abbot's token, a wooden tally cut two summers ago. He will sell at ten pence a pig to anyone who will try the crossing, and wants half the profit sworn to him.
Wigburh says a Dorestad skipper, Thiadbod, asked about the same lead and went away to think. She shows the clipped penny he paid with.
Offa's reeve can give a sealed word that the lead is the king's gift to his friend and no merchandise. He wants to know who else has asked.
At the abbot's own toll a Frisian boat with English lead is either a friend's errand or a broken ban, according to who is on the bank that day and what he is shown.
Eadhelm asks, without pressing, whether six pigs might stay for his own roof. He can pay in prayers and a burial plot.
With the kings at peace the lead may go openly. Beornoth has heard it already and the price is up; what was promised before still holds for the one who promised.
A scribe at York has Alcuin's own line about the quarrel of the kings. Copied fair and carried to the Dee, it is worth a penny a pig to the lead man.

endings.how: The merchant got the reeve's word at Lundenwic and landed the lead at Quentovic under it.
endings.text: The abbot's church is roofed with Mercian lead while two kings are not speaking. Beornoth is paid in silver for the first time in his life and buys a second ox.
endings.reward: About 300 d clear on forty pigs; Gervold's toll men know the boat; Beornoth sells to the house first at the old price for as long as he lives

endings.how: The merchant ran the lead across without leave and sold it where he could.
endings.text: It sells, for more. Gervold hears whose lead it was and who carried it, and says nothing aloud. Thiadbod hears too.
endings.reward: About 400 d; the toll at Quentovic is searched more closely from then on; Beornoth is content and the priest is not

endings.how: The merchant left a share of the lead for Saint John's, or bought it for the church.
endings.text: Eadhelm has a dry altar. He writes the merchant's name in the margin of his one gospel book, which is the only writing in the town.
endings.reward: The house may bury its dead at Saint John's; Eadhelm a fast friend; the work 'Lead on Saint John's roof' is counted as done

endings.how: Nothing was carried before the peace of 796.
endings.text: The ports open, the price rises, and a bigger hull from the south takes the whole stack in one lading. Beornoth nods to the merchant after that and keeps nothing back.
endings.reward: Nothing but the ordinary trade in lead at the market price

stories.reward: A standing source of lead at the digger's price, a name with the abbot who keeps the Frankish tolls, or a grave and a friend on the cliff.

stories.title: A leaf about this place
stories.summary: The priest of Saint John's has heard that Bede wrote of his city and has never seen the words. He wants one leaf copied in the north and carried home, and he has almost nothing to pay with.
stories.picture: A thin priest at the door of a small stone church on a red cliff, holding out both empty hands and smiling, a grassed-over amphitheatre hollow behind him.

beats.text: Eadhelm tells what he was told as a boy: a city of legions, a battle, monks cut down at prayer. He asks whether the merchant ever lies at a house where Bede is kept.
At Bede's own house the book is on the shelf. A scribe will copy the one chapter for a price in calfskin or wax, and thinks it odd that a priest should want only the part about himself.
At the minster Sigewine knows the priest's yearly letter by its hand. He will have the leaf made for nothing if the merchant carries something else for him on the way.
A Welsh herdsman at the crossing, hearing what is being fetched, says his people need no leaf: they have the names of the dead by heart, and a different count.
The leaf is read aloud at the church door on Saint John's day, in English, a line at a time. Nobody under the wall knew they lived anywhere that was in a book.

endings.how: The merchant had the leaf copied and brought it dry to the cliff.
endings.text: Eadhelm keeps it inside his gospel book and teaches the lead man's younger son to read from it. He teaches the merchant too, a letter a visit.
endings.reward: Eadhelm a fast friend; he teaches the Latin letters over three visits (learn latin); a name among the scribes of the north; the flag bk_carried if it was not already set

endings.how: The merchant brought the leaf and brought the Welshman to hear it read.
endings.text: The reading ends in an argument about numbers that lasts until dark and ends in the ale-house. After it the herdsmen trade at the bank more easily, and bring a monk's name for the priest to pray for.
endings.reward: As 'brought', and honey, hides and cattle from the Welsh side come to the bank a tenth cheaper for the house

endings.how: The merchant had the leaf made and sold it elsewhere, or never fetched it.
endings.text: Eadhelm asks once more, at midsummer, and then stops asking. He dies with two books. The next priest cannot read either.
endings.reward: The price of a leaf, about 20 d; after 814 nobody at Saint John's can read a letter for the house

stories.reward: A priest who knows the house by name, his letters, and a place for the house's dead on the cliff.

stories.title: The waste city wakes
stories.summary: Northmen driven from Dublin sit on the Wirral shore by the Lady's leave and look at the walls she is mending. Both sides buy from the merchant, both ask him what the other is doing, and one morning there is smoke.
stories.picture: Men on a new-mended red wall tipping a steaming cauldron and a straw beehive over the edge, attackers below under hurdles covered with hides; a woman in a white head-cloth watching from a gate tower.

beats.text: The fort at the black pool is taken. People wade out to anything that floats. Some of those the merchant carries off, or refuses, will be on the Wirral shore within the year.
Hingamund buys hides, ale and seed corn and pays in Irish silver by weight. He asks, lightly, how high the south wall stands these days.
The Lady asks how many ships lie on the north shore. She has a word she wants carried to the Irish among the Northmen, who are Christians: that they are remembered, and by whom.

The townsmen are counting what they have that will pour or sting: brewing cauldrons, and every straw hive in the gardens. The merchant has honey and ale aboard, or hides, and each is wanted by a different side.
The tale is told in the ale-house with more ale and more bees every year. The bee-keepers have not yet been paid for their hives.
Word at York: the people of the city have promised to hold to the Lady. Before midsummer she is dead at Tamworth, and the promise with her.

Nine years before the men of Dublin come, a Danish army rides across England and shuts itself inside the empty walls. The English burn the corn all round, and by spring the army has gone into Wales for want of food.

endings.how: The merchant carried the Lady's word to the Irish and sold his ale and honey inside the walls.
endings.text: The attack fails. The Lady has a plot marked out for the house on the street to the river and tells the reeve the boat pays nothing at her gate.
endings.reward: The unlock 'a burgess of the Lady's burh' (the plot, and no toll here while she lives); about 250 d for the cargo; the Wirral men cool for some years

endings.how: The merchant sold hides and food to Hingamund and told the Lady nothing she could use.
endings.text: The attack fails all the same. Hingamund's people stay on their sand, grow barley, and remember who fed them in the first winters.
endings.reward: A friend on the Wirral shore: trade at the beach past the point without the reeve, and a good word in Dublin when the fort is taken back in 917; the Lady's hall closed to the house until 918

endings.how: The merchant sold to both and carried word for both.
endings.text: Each side finds out, as each side always does. Nobody harms him. Nobody tells him anything again.
endings.reward: The most silver of the three, about 400 d; no friend on either side, and prices a tenth worse at both for five years

endings.how: The merchant stayed out of the river until it was over.
endings.text: He hears of it in another port as a story about bees, and does not believe it.
endings.reward: Nothing gained or lost; the tale can be traded as news once

stories.reward: A plot and a free gate in a town about to become the richest mint in the west, or a friend among the people who will be Dublin's traders.

stories.title: The Ireland-farer's pennies
stories.summary: The moneyer Irfara strikes pennies with no king's head so that Dublin will take them, and wants Dublin's broken silver back to melt. Between his bench, the reeve's first look at the marten skins, and the beach past the point where no reeve stands, there are three ways to grow rich and two to lose a ship.
stories.picture: A wiry man at a moneyer's block holding a new penny up to the light of a doorway, a folding balance round his neck, a pot of clippings at his elbow.

beats.text: Irfara weighs the merchant's silver, nicks it, and offers new pennies at a small loss. He will forgo the loss for a man who brings him hacked silver from over the water.
In Dublin the plain pennies pass by weight and are liked. Arm-rings and cut silver are cheap there, and marten skins cheaper than anywhere a Frisian knows.
The reeve sees marten skins before anyone and takes what the king wants at the king's price. Forty shillings from the man who does not show them.
A pilot offers, without quite saying it, the beach on the tip of Wirral: no board, no reeve, no four pence. And no witness if a sale goes wrong.
At York a bale from the west is opened with a lead tag still on its cord, struck from Chester dies. Goods that crossed the hills under the reeve's seal are not asked about twice.
The king's new coin: the old pennies are called in, and of twenty benches five are left. A house that holds old silver must bring it now or pass it by weight for ever.

endings.how: The merchant brought good silver three times, showed every skin, and paid the four pence.
endings.text: The moneyer changes the house's silver at no loss, and the reeve's men wave the boat to her old berth without coming aboard. The heirs inherit both habits.
endings.reward: The unlock 'the moneyers' trust'; goods sent on to York under the reeve's tag; a steady 150 to 250 d a voyage on marten and salt

endings.how: The merchant took his skins and silver by the beach past the point.
endings.text: It pays better for some years. Then a reeve's man is at the beach one morning, dressed as a fisherman, and counts the crew.
endings.reward: Half as much again on each voyage while it lasts; when caught, forty shillings from every man aboard, or the ship; the Wirral men think the better of him

endings.how: The merchant sold clipped or foreign silver into the town as good.
endings.text: A light penny is traced to the house. Irfara will not look at him. The twelve judges do.
endings.reward: A quick 100 d; then a fine at the judges' word and the mint shut to the house for a generation

stories.reward: Silver changed at no loss at the busiest mint in the west, and a lawful road for Irish goods over the hills to York.

stories.title: Six kings, or eight
stories.summary: In 973 King Edgar brings every ship he has to the Dee and six kings come to swear to him. A fleet eats, the reeve needs witnesses who can count, and for the rest of the story the tale grows in every ale-house the house visits.
stories.picture: A river crowded with ships under red walls, pennons out, and on the bank a stout reeve counting crowned men on his fingers while a merchant looks on.

beats.text: The reeve has a fleet to feed and no time. He will buy grain, ale, salt meat and cheese at any honest price and waive the four pence for whoever brings them first.
Six kings come to the bank and covenant with the king to be his allies by sea and by land. The merchant can stand among the witnesses, if he is known, and count them himself.
The canons say the king was rowed up the river to their church. A year on, some say the kings took the oars. Nobody who was on the bank says so.
In Dublin the same day is told as a meeting of equals, and the count of kings is whatever suits the teller's lord.
Ships out of the north are in the shire. A man by the north wall asks the merchant to take his pennies down the river, or help him put them under the floor.
Eight kings now, each with an oar, and the king at the helm. The merchant's own grandfather is in the tale, selling them cheese.

endings.how: The merchant brought provisions in 973 and stood witness.
endings.text: The reeve remembers who fed the king's ships. The house is named in the port as one that comes by the king's leave, and need not ask it again.
endings.reward: The unlock 'the king's leave on the Dee'; about 500 d on the cargo; the true count of kings, which can be told as news for years

endings.how: In 980 the merchant carried the man's silver to safety and brought it back.
endings.text: The man lives, digs nothing up, and stands surety for the house before the twelve judges whenever it is needed.
endings.reward: A surety in the town (a delay on one debt, once in each generation); a tenth of the silver, about 50 d, pressed on him

endings.how: In 980 the merchant helped bury the pot and the man did not come back.
endings.text: Only the house knows where it lies. It can be fetched, and it can be left for whoever finds it in a thousand years.
endings.reward: A buried hoard to fetch (open_fetch), some 120 pennies; or, left alone, the easter egg under the north wall stays true

endings.how: The merchant was not there, and tells the tale with eight kings anyway.
endings.text: It is a better story. People buy him ale for it from Dublin to London.
endings.reward: Free drink wherever the tale is new; the reeve at Chester, who counted six, never quite trusts his word

stories.reward: The king's leave on the Dee, a surety before the judges, or a pot of pennies under a floor.

works.name: Lead on Saint John's roof
works.what: Sheets beaten from Beornoth's pigs and nailed over the church on the cliff in place of rotten shingles, with a gutter to carry the rain off the altar end.
works.picture: Two men on a small stone church roof beating a grey sheet flat with wooden mallets, a priest below holding the ladder and looking up.
works.needs: Sixteen pigs of lead bought from Beornoth or brought back; Eadhelm or his successor willing
works.gives: The priest of Saint John's a friend to the house and its heirs; burial there for the house's dead; the church can shelter cargo in a wet season
works.source: Invented. Lead for church roofs: Bede has Bishop Eadberht roof Lindisfarne in lead (HE III.25, memory (?)); Design/content/economy/stone_metal_arms.md. The price is the game's

works.name: A staithe on the mud
works.what: Oak piles driven into the bank below the south wall and a deck of split logs over them, so that a boat can load at half tide without her crew wading.
works.picture: A short rough timber stage standing out over red mud at low water, a small boat alongside, men rolling a grey lead pig down a plank.
works.needs: Osfrith's word on where the channel will stay; oak from up the river
works.gives: Loading and unloading here take half the time; no porters needed for lead; after 907 the reeve counts it as the house's own berth
works.source: Invented. The early harbour on the bank below Lower Bridge Street: VCH Cheshire 5.1. No timber staging of these years has been found (?)

works.name: A rod of the new wall
works.what: One measured length of the wall the Lady is running from the corner of the fortress down to the river, paid for in stone carted, lime burned and men fed.
works.picture: Masons setting red blocks on a half-built wall that runs downhill to a river, a tally-keeper with notched sticks, carts of stone waiting.
works.needs: The leave of the Lady or, after her, the reeve; the story 'The waste city wakes' not ended on the shore
works.gives: The house is counted among the burgesses: a voice before the twelve judges, and shelter inside the walls with its goods when ships are in the river
works.source: The wall probably run from the south-east corner to the river after 907: VCH Cheshire 5.1. Before 1066 the reeve called a man from every hide to mend the wall and the bridge: Domesday Book (memory (?)). A merchant paying for a length is the game's

works.name: A cellared house on the river street
works.what: A timber house with a dug cellar on the street that goes down to the landing, among the bow-sided huts of the Dublin men: dry storage under a floor that locks.
works.picture: A timber house on a sloping street with an open trapdoor showing a plank-lined cellar full of sacks and pots, the river at the street's foot.
works.needs: A plot: bought, or given by the Lady
works.gives: A store of the house's own here (salt, pots and skins held between voyages at no rent); a bed; a place in the rent roll of the town
works.source: Cellared buildings and bow-sided huts on Lower Bridge Street in the 10th century: VCH Cheshire 5.1 (the cellars from the dossier's memory (?))

works.name: A round-headed cross at Saint John's
works.what: A grave cross cut by the masons of Saint John's from the red rock of the cliff, its head a ring with a boss, to stand over the house's dead.
works.picture: A waist-high red sandstone cross with a ring head standing in rough grass by a church wall, a mason brushing dust from the carving.
works.needs: One of the house buried at Saint John's, or a death at sea to remember
works.gives: The house's dead are remembered here by name (act remember costs nothing and steadies the crew); the canons of Saint John's friendly
works.source: The circle-headed crosses of the St John's masons' yard, found also in Wirral and Flintshire, 10th to 11th century (?): VCH Cheshire 5.1

ships.how: bought second-hand from the fishermen of the Dee, or built over a winter if you find the oak
ships.note: The river's own boat: for salmon, for the ferry, for carrying lead pigs down to a ship in the channel.
ships.picture: A tarred open boat on red mud with a salmon net heaped in her stern and a sounding pole laid across the thwarts.
ships.source: No boat of these years has been found at Chester; the class from ship_classes_793.json. Salmon in the Dee is ordinary knowledge (?)

ships.how: bought from the Welsh or Irish who come up the river, for cattle or salt
ships.note: Hide boats work this river and the coast to the west; a man can carry a small one on his back past the sands.
ships.picture: A black hide boat upturned on stakes to dry, its wicker ribs showing through, a herdsman greasing the seams.
ships.source: Hide boats on the Welsh rivers and the Irish Sea are well attested in general; none is recorded at Chester (?). The class from ship_classes_793.json

ships.how: bought from the settlers on the Wirral shore, or built by them to order over a winter
ships.note: The Northmen out of Dublin brought their boats and their boat-builders; a six-oar boat is what they cross the river mouth in.
ships.picture: A slim clinker boat with six oars on a sandy shore, a bow-sided hut and a drying rack of fish behind her.
ships.source: Norse settlement in Wirral from 902: VCH Cheshire 5.1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingimundr_(tenth_century). Boat-building there is inferred (?)

ships.how: bought second-hand from a Dublin or Manx skipper, or hired with her crew for one crossing
ships.note: The ship of the Dublin trade: she brings marten skins and takes salt, pots and people. One comes up for sale when a skipper has been fined more than he has.
ships.picture: A sixteen-metre clinker ship with her mast lowered, lying at a river landing under red walls, bales of skins being handed up.
ships.source: Dublin and Manx Norse boats at Chester; the fines of the port: VCH Cheshire 5.1 and Domesday (memory (?)). That ships were sold to pay fines is the game's

sayings.source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 907 (Ingram 1823), as the dossier gives it; said in the town of anything mended at last, a roof or a marriage

sayings.text: There came to meet him six kings; and they all covenanted with him, that they would be his allies by sea and by land.
Six kings swore. Eight rowed. By the time my son tells it they will have carried the boat.
sayings.source: Invented in the period's manner: the Chronicle has six kings and no boat; the rowing is in 12th-century writers

sayings.text: A friend is good far or near, but the nearer is the handier.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, own rendering from the Old English 'Freond deah feor ge neah: byth near nyttra'; said of the Dublin men

sayings.text: After mead men are often thirstiest.
sayings.source: Durham Proverbs, own rendering from the Old English 'Hwilum aefter medo menn maest gethyrsteth'; Wigburh's, when a man asks for one more

sayings.text: The Romans built for giants and we keep pigs in it.
sayings.source: Invented in the period's manner, after the Old English poem The Ruin and its 'work of giants' (not quoted)

sayings.text: Ask a Dublin man the price of marten and he will ask you who is reeve.
sayings.source: Invented in the period's manner: the reeve's first sight of marten skins, Domesday Chester (memory (?))

sayings.text: She chose the dung-stool. She said the shillings would last longer.
sayings.source: Invented, on the fine for bad ale in the city's customs before 1066: the stool or four shillings (Domesday, memory (?))

easter_eggs.text: On the quarry face across the river a small carved woman holds a spear, with an owl at her shoulder. Nobody under the wall knows her name. The herdsmen's children leave her a flower at lambing and are slapped for it.
easter_eggs.source: The rock-cut shrine of Minerva in the Roman quarry at Handbridge, still in place today: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deva_Victrix. The flowers are invented; no cult is known

easter_eggs.text: Some of the pigs Beornoth digs up by the old workings have letters cast along their backs. He cannot read them. They are the name of a people who lived in those hills, and the year of an emperor.
easter_eggs.source: Roman lead pigs stamped with the name of the Deceangli have been found at and near Chester (memory (?))

easter_eggs.text: A brooch on the board at the cross and a brooch in a Dublin woman's cloak are from one mould. Whoever looks at both knows which town the smith went home to.
easter_eggs.source: A Borre-style brooch from Princess Street, Chester, from the same mould as one found in Dublin: VCH Cheshire 5.1

easter_eggs.text: A moneyer here signs his pennies Irfara: the Ireland-farer. He is the only man in the port who puts on the king's coin where he has been.
They say the saint in the minster once brought a goose back to life after it had been eaten, bones and all, and scolded the man who ate it. The geese of the town are not grateful.
easter_eggs.source: Goscelin's Life of Werburgh (11th century), via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werburgh

easter_eggs.text: By the south-west corner of the wall, a little after 965, the earth is fresh over a pot. Five hundred pennies, some ingots, a cut arm-ring. Its owner does not come back in this story or in any other.
easter_eggs.source: The Castle Esplanade hoard, buried about 965, found 1950: VCH Cheshire 5.1

easter_eggs.text: Nobody alive knows who Henwald was. The mound has his name, the sheep have his grass, and the thorn on top has outlived three kings.
A lead tag on a cord, struck with a penny die of this town, turns up on a bale at York. It is how a reeve says 'I have seen this' across sixty miles of hill.
easter_eggs.source: A lead customs tag from Chester dies of Eadwig's reign (955-959), found at Coppergate, York: VCH Cheshire 5.1

unlocks.what: Beornoth's word: lead at the digger's price, kept back for the house
unlocks.how: End 'Lead for the abbot's roof' by the seal or the roof; or buy from him in three different years without beating him below ten pence
unlocks.gives: lead here at two thirds of the market price until 811, and from his sons at four fifths after; six pigs always held for the house

unlocks.what: a bench at Wigburh's: she knows the crew by name and keeps the house's news
unlocks.how: Lodge at the baths in three different years and pay what is owed each time, your lookout's cup included
unlocks.gives: lodging and rumours here cost nothing; she holds messages for the house; she says who asked about you, and one true thing about Thiadbod's dealings each year

unlocks.what: the Latin letters, taught by the priest of Saint John's
unlocks.how: End 'A leaf about this place' with the leaf brought
unlocks.gives: learn latin; burial at Saint John's; flag bk_carried

unlocks.what: a burgess of the Lady's burh: a plot on the river street and a free gate
unlocks.how: End 'The waste city wakes' as the Lady's man, or pay for a rod of the new wall
unlocks.gives: flag legacaestir_burgess; no toll at the water gate until 918 and half after; the work 'A cellared house on the river street' needs no plot bought

unlocks.what: the moneyers' trust: silver changed at no loss
unlocks.how: End 'The Ireland-farer's pennies' by true weight
unlocks.gives: flag legacaestir_mint_trust; change_coin here at no loss; goods may go on to Eoforwic under the reeve's tag, toll paid once

unlocks.what: the king's leave on the Dee: the boat comes and goes unasked
unlocks.how: Feed the fleet in 973 and stand witness; held by the heirs while the four pence is paid
unlocks.gives: flag legacaestir_kings_leave; no question of leave at the reeve's board; marten skins are still shown first, but at a price a tenth better

unlocks.what: the beach past the point: the Wirral men's market, without a reeve
unlocks.how: End 'The waste city wakes' on the shore, or hire Osfrith as pilot three times and ask him plainly
unlocks.gives: sales of skins and silver without the four pence, at a risk the card names (doubtful after 958); a welcome among the Northmen of the Wirral
